analysis.one_liner: Gives survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault up to 30 days of job-protected leave, unemployment access, and insurance safeguards.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill had one Democratic sponsor and eight Democratic cosponsors, but the Senate committee it went to never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more workers to give survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking up to 30 days of leave in a year — part of it paid, earned at one hour for every 30 hours worked — to seek medical care, counseling, safety planning, relocation, or legal help. It would make it illegal to fire or penalize someone for being a survivor or for taking part in a court case related to the abuse, guarantee survivors access to unemployment benefits if they have to leave a job because of the violence, and bar insurers from denying coverage, raising premiums, or dropping a survivor from a plan because of the abuse. It would also reauthorize federal grants that help employers and survivor-services organizations handle violence in the workplace.
analysis.who_benefits: Survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking — most often women, along with their family members — who would get protected time off to escape abuse or go to court, protection from being fired for their status as survivors, guaranteed access to unemployment benefits if violence forces them out of a job, and insurance protections that keep abusers from cutting off their coverage through divorce or separation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Survivors of domestic and sexual violence

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide each worker up to 30 days of safe leave in a 12-month period, including at least one hour of paid leave earned per 30 hours worked (capped at 56 hours banked at a time), usable for medical care, counseling, safety planning, relocation, or legal proceedings [S3].

Employers and public agencies may not fire, refuse to hire, or otherwise discriminate against someone because they are or are perceived to be a survivor, because they participate in a court proceeding, or because they ask for a reasonable safety accommodation at work, with damages and attorney's fees for violations [S3].

States may not deny unemployment compensation to someone who left a job because of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking, and may not impose extra conditions beyond what applies to anyone else forced to leave a job, with a sworn statement alone sufficient documentation [S3].

Insurers may not deny, cancel, or limit coverage, charge premium surcharges, or deny claims because the applicant or insured is a survivor, and may not terminate a survivor's health coverage after a divorce or separation from the abuser who held the policy [S3].

States may use welfare-block-grant (TANF) funds for short-term emergency benefits paid on an expedited basis to people taking safe leave, and federal grants are authorized to train unemployment and welfare staff on handling survivor claims confidentially [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more workers bear the cost of providing and covering work during the new leave, especially the paid portion, and face damages and fee liability if they discriminate or interfere with leave. Health, life, disability, and property insurers lose the ability to price, deny, or drop coverage based on a survivor's experience of abuse and must continue coverage after a divorce or separation. The public Treasury would fund a training-grant program authorized at $1 million in 2018 and $12 million a year for 2019-2022.
analysis.who_pays_short: Midsize and large employers and insurers

drawbacks.text: The paid-leave accrual requirement applies to every employer with 15 or more employees, a threshold that includes many small businesses, and unpaid safe leave is in addition to leave already allowed under the Family and Medical Leave Act, so an employer could face an employee absent for 30 days on top of 12 weeks of FMLA time [S3].

The bill lets employers require certification of the need for leave, but accepts flexible forms including a sworn statement from the employee or documentation from an advocate, attorney, or member of the clergy, which critics could argue is easy to assert and hard for an employer to verify, with liquidated damages doubling the employer's exposure for a violation [S3].

The mandate is an unfunded employer obligation: apart from the training grants, the bill provides no federal money to offset leave costs, and the emergency-benefit option leaves it up to each state whether to use its welfare funds that way [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in four women and one in nine men the bill text cites as having experienced intimate-partner violence or stalking, the protections address a documented gap: federal law on the books did not explicitly authorize survivors to take leave for safety or legal matters, guarantee them unemployment benefits, or bar insurers from discriminating against them [S3]. The costs fall on covered employers and insurers and are real but limited — the paid portion is capped at 56 banked hours, employers can demand certification, and the highest-paid 10% of workers can be denied reinstatement in narrow circumstances [S3]. The bill's main weakness is not its design but its reach: it was never amended, scored, or negotiated, so the compliance burden on smaller covered employers was never tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the bill on October 31, 2017, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors: Blumenthal, Baldwin, Klobuchar, Franken, Feinstein, Hirono, Leahy, and Cardin [S1] [S4].

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and insurers are better off because the bill died: they avoided a paid safe-leave mandate, discrimination liability with double damages, and a prohibition on pricing or dropping coverage based on a customer's experience of abuse. Survivors gained nothing, since no version of these protections became law in that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers; survivors gained nothing

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the record shows no action after referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All nine senators behind the bill were Democrats, no Republican cosponsor joined, and the Republican-chaired committee to which it was referred never acted on it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill imposes a new paid-leave accrual (one hour per 30 worked, up to 56 banked hours), up to 30 days of leave on top of existing entitlements, a duty to accommodate safety requests, and discrimination liability with liquidated damages. Employers' interest in avoiding these obligations runs against the survivors the bill protects.

industries.industry: Health, life, disability, and property insurers
industries.note: Insurers would be barred from denying, canceling, or limiting coverage, adding premium surcharges, or denying claims because a customer is a survivor, and from cutting off a survivor's health coverage after a divorce or separation from the policyholding abuser. Their ability to price and underwrite based on abuse history would end.

The bill reauthorizes federal grants for these nonprofits to advise employers and workers, and authorizes a training-grant program at $1 million in 2018 and $12 million a year through 2022 to prepare unemployment and welfare staff to handle survivor claims. Their funding interest runs with the interests of the people they serve.
